To "go for broke" means to risk everything you have — all your energy, money, effort, or resources — in one bold attempt to achieve something. You hold nothing back. You commit completely, knowing that if you fail, you could end up with nothing.

Think of it this way: you are putting all your chips on the table. You are not playing it safe. You are going all in, with the full understanding that you might lose everything, but also that this is your best — or perhaps only — shot at winning big.

To understand an idiom well, it helps to look at the individual words.

"Broke" is a common informal word for having no money at all. If someone says "I'm broke," they mean their wallet is empty.

"Go for" in this context means to aim for or to attempt to reach something.

So, "go for broke" literally paints a picture of someone saying: "I am willing to risk becoming completely broke — losing everything — in order to win." It is the act of staking everything on a single attempt.

This idiom has its roots in gambling slang, likely originating in the early 20th century in the United States. In gambling, if you go for broke, you bet every single dollar you have on one hand, one roll, or one outcome. There is no backup plan. You either win big or walk away with nothing.

However, the phrase became truly famous because of a real-life group of heroes during World War II.

The 442nd Regimental Combat Team was a unit made up almost entirely of Japanese-American soldiers. Many of these men volunteered to fight for the United States even while their own families were being held in internment camps back home — a painful and deeply unjust situation. Despite this, they chose to prove their loyalty and courage.

They adopted "Go for Broke" as their official battle motto. To them, it meant giving absolutely everything — holding nothing in reserve — to win. And win they did. The 442nd became one of the most decorated military units in the entire history of the United States Army, earning over 18,000 individual decorations for bravery.

Their story turned the phrase from a gambling term into a celebrated expression of total commitment and fearless sacrifice. In 1951, a Hollywood film titled Go for Broke! was made in their honor, which helped spread the phrase into everyday American language.
The Core Feeling of the Idiom

"Go for broke" captures a very specific human feeling: the moment when you decide that playing it safe is no longer an option, and you throw caution to the wind.

It combines three powerful ideas:

  • Total commitment — you are not half-hearted.
  • Accepted risk — you know you might fail or lose everything.
  • A desire to win or succeed — the risk is taken with a purpose, not carelessly.

It is important to note that "go for broke" is not reckless stupidity. The phrase carries a tone of bold, intentional courage. The person using it understands the risk and chooses to accept it anyway, because the goal is worth it.
How It Is Used in Real Life

The idiom can be used in many different situations — sports, business, personal decisions, competitions, and more. Here are some clear examples:

In sports:

"We are down by two goals with five minutes left. It's time to go for broke — pull the goalkeeper and push everyone forward."

Here, the team is abandoning their defensive strategy entirely and risking giving up more goals, all in hopes of scoring enough to win.

In business:

"She invested every penny of her savings into her startup. She decided to go for broke because she truly believed in her idea."

She risked financial ruin, holding nothing back, to pursue her dream.

In a personal challenge:

"He had been training for the marathon for a year. On race day, he decided to go for broke and run at his fastest pace from the very start."

He risked exhausting himself completely, but he wanted to give his very best.

In an exam or competition:

"I only have thirty minutes left and I haven't answered the hardest questions yet. I'm going to go for broke and write as much as I can."
The Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Go for broke" is a verb phrase (an idiom built around a verb). Here is how it changes based on the subject and tense:

  • Present: I / We / They go for broke. He / She goes for broke.
  • Past: She went for broke.
  • Future: They will go for broke.
  • Present continuous (right now): We are going for broke.
  • As a command / suggestion: "Go for broke!" or "Let's go for broke."

It is almost always used with the verbs go, went, going — you do not normally change "broke" to anything else.

This idiom is informal and conversational. You would comfortably use it with friends, in sports commentary, in casual writing, in motivational speeches, and in everyday storytelling.

You would generally avoid it in very formal or academic writing, though it can appear in business contexts when the writing style is energetic and informal.

The tone it carries is almost always positive and exciting — it suggests bravery, passion, and full commitment. It is rarely used in a negative or criticizing way.
Similar Idioms and Phrases (So You Can Compare)

Understanding related expressions will help you see exactly where "go for broke" sits:

  • "All in" — Very similar. Comes from poker; means committing everything.
  • "Pull out all the stops" — Means to use every possible effort or resource. (Less risky in tone; more about giving maximum effort.)
  • "Throw caution to the wind" — Means to take a risk and ignore the potential dangers. (More impulsive in tone, less goal-driven.)
  • "Bet the farm" — Means to risk everything, usually in a business or financial context. (More specific to financial risk.)
  • "Give it everything you've got" — Means to put in maximum effort. (No implied risk of loss; just about effort level.)

"Go for broke" sits at the intersection of maximum effort and accepted risk of total loss. The others only capture one of these two aspects.
One Easy Way to Always Remember It

Picture a gambler sitting at a card table. He has been playing all night. He looks at his cards, takes a deep breath, and pushes every single chip he owns into the center of the table. His hands might be shaking. He knows he might walk out of that casino with empty pockets. But he also knows this is his best hand of the night, and he is not going to hold back.

That moment — that feeling — is "going for broke."

Whenever you hear or read this idiom, picture that gambler pushing all his chips forward. That image will never fail you.

MeaningTo risk everything in one bold, all-out attempt to succeed
ToneInformal, positive, bold, exciting
OriginGambling slang; famously adopted by the Japanese-American 442nd Regiment in WWII
Key ideaTotal commitment + accepted risk of total loss + desire to win
Use it whenDescribing someone giving everything they have, holding nothing back

"Go for broke" is ultimately a phrase about courage in the face of uncertainty. It is what you say — or feel — when playing it safe is simply not good enough, and the only way forward is to commit with your whole heart, your whole effort, and everything you have.
